analogy.p: Picture two floors joined by an up escalator and a down escalator. If 20 people ride up every minute and 20 ride down every minute, the number on each floor stays the same even though people are constantly moving. That matches dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse changes are both happening at equal rates, so totals are constant. There may be 100 people upstairs and 300 downstairs, which matches the idea that the amounts are constant but not necessarily equal. The analogy breaks down because people choose to move, whereas particles react because of collisions with enough energy, and their rates depend on concentration and temperature.
analogy.t: The escalator in a shopping centre

bullets: **Reversible reaction**: a reaction in which the products can react to produce the original reactants again.
The symbol is ⇌ (two half-arrows), not → ; always use it when you write the equation for a reversible reaction.
**Forward reaction** = reactants → products. **Reverse reaction** = products → reactants.
The terms 'forward' and 'reverse' depend only on how the equation is written; if you swap the sides of the equation, the names swap too.
Many reactions are only reversible under certain conditions; for example a reaction may be reversible in a sealed container but go to completion if a gas can escape.
Reversibility is the idea behind equilibrium: without a reverse reaction there can be no equilibrium.
Link to other topics: the Haber process (N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3) and the Contact process are reversible reactions, which is why industrial chemists must choose conditions carefully to get a good yield.
core.p: Most reactions you meet at GCSE are written with a single arrow because they go to completion: the reactants are used up and turn into products. In a **reversible reaction** the products can react with each other to re-form the original reactants, so the reaction can go in both directions. We show this with the symbol ⇌ in the equation, for example A + B ⇌ C + D. The reaction from left to right is called the **forward reaction** and the reaction from right to left is the **reverse reaction**. Both can happen at the same time in the same container.

bullets: Hydrated copper sulfate: CuSO4.5H2O(s) ⇌ CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l). Blue (hydrated) ⇌ white (anhydrous) + water.
Heating the blue crystals: water is driven off (thermal decomposition) and the solid turns white. This is the forward reaction and it is endothermic.
Adding a few drops of water to the white powder: it turns blue again and the tube gets hot. This is the reverse reaction and it is exothermic.
Ammonium chloride: NH4Cl(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + HCl(g). On heating, the white solid disappears from the bottom of the test tube.
Higher in the tube, where it is cooler, the ammonia and hydrogen chloride react together and white ammonium chloride solid re-forms (the reverse reaction).
Haber process: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). Nitrogen and hydrogen make ammonia, but ammonia also breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen.
Nitrogen dioxide / dinitrogen tetroxide: N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g) is a useful exam example because the colour changes (colourless to brown) show which way the position has moved.
Not every thermal decomposition is reversible; only if the products can meet and react again (in a closed system or when they stay in contact).
core.h: Examples of reversible reactions you must know
core.p: AQA expects you to know that reversible reactions are shown by ⇌ and to be able to use simple examples. Two classic laboratory examples involve a colour or state change that you can see happening in both directions. Heating **hydrated copper(II) sulfate** (blue crystals) drives off water to leave **anhydrous copper(II) sulfate** (white powder); adding water to the white powder gives back the blue solid. Heating **ammonium chloride** makes it break up into ammonia and hydrogen chloride gas; on cooling, the two gases recombine as solid ammonium chloride.

bullets: If the forward reaction is exothermic (releases energy to the surroundings), the reverse reaction is endothermic (takes in energy) by the same amount.
Worked example: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 releases 92 kJ per mole of equation as written; so 2NH3 → N2 + 3H2 takes in 92 kJ.
Hydrated copper sulfate: heating (forward, endothermic) takes in energy; adding water (reverse, exothermic) releases the same amount of energy as heat.
Exothermic = temperature of surroundings rises. Endothermic = temperature of surroundings falls.
On a reaction profile the forward and reverse reactions are the same curve read in opposite directions; the energy difference between reactants and products is the same size.
Do not say 'the energy is used up'; say 'energy is transferred to / from the surroundings'.
Link to other topics: energy changes (4.5) and bond energies; the same logic explains why raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction.
core.p: If a reversible reaction is **exothermic** in one direction, it is **endothermic** in the opposite direction. The amount of energy transferred is **exactly the same** in both directions; only the direction of transfer is different. This follows from the conservation of energy: the energy released when bonds form in one direction must equal the energy needed to break the same bonds in the other. This idea is the key to Le Chatelier's principle for temperature changes (Higher tier), so learn it thoroughly.

bullets: **Closed system**: no particles can leave or enter, so everything made stays in the container and can take part in the reverse reaction.
**Open system**: matter can leave, so a gas product is lost and the reaction cannot be reversible in practice.
Example: CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g). In a sealed tube CO2 stays and recombines with CaO, so equilibrium is reached. In an open tube CO2 escapes and the reaction goes to completion.
Heat can still enter or leave a closed system; 'closed' refers to matter, not energy.
Industrial reactors such as the Haber reactor behave as closed systems because the gases are kept under pressure in a sealed vessel.
If the question says 'closed system', mention it in your answer; it is often worth a mark.
A system in equilibrium that is opened to the air will change, because particles escape or enter and the balance is lost.
core.p: A reversible reaction can only reach equilibrium in a **closed system**, which is one where none of the reactants or products can escape and nothing can enter. A sealed flask or a stoppered tube is a closed system. In an **open system** (such as an open test tube) a gaseous product can escape into the air; the reverse reaction then cannot take place and the reaction runs on to completion. This is why the exam repeatedly uses the phrase 'in a closed system'.

bullets: Definition to write in an exam: 'In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.'
Consequence: the amounts (concentrations) of reactants and products do not change.
'Dynamic' = both reactions are still happening. Never write that the reaction 'has stopped'.
The concentrations are constant but **not necessarily equal**; there may be much more product than reactant, or the other way round.
Equilibrium can be approached from either side: start with only reactants, only products, or any mixture, and the same equilibrium composition is reached under the same conditions.
Equal rates does not mean zero rates: both rates are greater than zero at equilibrium.
Link to other topics: rates of reaction (collision theory) explains why the rates change as concentrations change; the rate of a reaction depends on concentration.
core.p: In a closed system, **dynamic equilibrium** is reached when the **forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate**. At that point the **concentrations of reactants and products stay constant**, even though both reactions are still going on. The word 'dynamic' means moving or changing: at the particle level reactants are turning into products and products are turning back into reactants all the time, but the two changes cancel out so there is no overall change that we can measure. Learn this as a two-part answer: equal rates, constant concentrations.

bullets: Start: concentration of A is high, so forward rate is high; concentration of B is zero, so reverse rate is zero.
As time passes: [A] falls so forward rate falls; [B] rises so reverse rate rises.
At equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate; [A] and [B] are constant.
Why the forward rate falls: fewer particles of A per unit volume, so fewer collisions per second, so fewer successful collisions per second.
Why the reverse rate rises: more particles of B per unit volume, so more collisions per second.
Equilibrium is reached more quickly if the rates are faster, for example at higher temperature or with a catalyst.
The time taken to reach equilibrium and the position of equilibrium are different ideas: do not mix them up.
Link to other topics: the curve of concentration against time becomes horizontal in the same way as a rate-of-reaction graph levelling off, but here the reaction has not stopped.
core.h: How equilibrium is reached, step by step
core.p: Imagine a closed flask that starts with only reactant A for the reaction A ⇌ B. At the start the concentration of A is at its highest, so the forward reaction is at its fastest. There is no B yet, so the reverse reaction has a rate of zero. As A is used, its concentration falls and the forward rate slows; as B builds up, the reverse rate speeds up. Eventually the two rates become equal and the system is at dynamic equilibrium. This is a very common exam explanation, and it is built on collision theory: more concentrated particles collide more often, so reaction is faster.

bullets: Both lines are horizontal (parallel to the time axis) at equilibrium: the concentrations are constant.
The lines do not have to cross, and they are not usually at the same height: constant is not the same as equal.
Time to equilibrium: read off where the lines first become flat, and quote the time with units.
Relative amounts: compare the heights of the horizontal parts to say whether more reactants or more products are present.
Steepness at the start shows the initial rate; a steeper line means a faster change.
If a condition is then changed (see Le Chatelier, Higher tier), the lines move to new horizontal levels after a short curved section.
If the reactant starts at 1.0 mol/dm3 for A ⇌ B and reaches 0.4 mol/dm3, then B is 0.6 mol/dm3 (one-to-one ratio), so the position lies to the right.
Common marks: 'concentrations become constant' and 'equilibrium reached after ... s'.
core.p: A graph of concentration against time for a reversible reaction in a closed system shows the reactant falling and the product rising until both lines become **horizontal**. The time at which the lines first become horizontal is when equilibrium has been reached. The vertical gap between the two lines at that point tells you the relative amounts: if the product line is higher, the equilibrium mixture contains more product than reactant (the position lies to the right). Always read values from the graph, because data-based marks are common.

bullets: Forward rate: starts at a maximum and decreases as reactant is used up.
Reverse rate: starts at zero (no product yet) and increases as product builds up.
The lines meet at the time equilibrium is reached, and after that stay level and together.
Labelling: always label which line is forward and which is reverse, and label the axes 'rate' and 'time'.
If you are asked to sketch the graph from products only, the lines are swapped: reverse rate starts high, forward rate starts at zero.
After equilibrium, both rates are not zero; the reaction continues in both directions.
Link to other topics: the same ideas appear in Le Chatelier's principle (Higher tier), where a change makes the two rates unequal until a new equilibrium is reached.
core.p: You can also plot the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction against time. Starting with reactants only, the forward rate begins high and falls, while the reverse rate begins at zero and rises. The two lines meet and then continue together as a single horizontal line: from that point the rates are equal, which is the definition of dynamic equilibrium. The common value of the rates at equilibrium is greater than zero. This graph explains the shape of the concentration graph, so make sure you can link the two.

bullets: **Position of equilibrium**: the relative amounts of reactants and products in the equilibrium mixture.
Position 'to the right' = more products; 'to the left' = more reactants.
Different conditions give different equilibrium compositions for the same reaction.
A **catalyst** speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but the position does not change.
Yield is a percentage: percentage yield = actual amount of product / maximum theoretical amount of product × 100.
The position of equilibrium tells you the maximum yield you could get under those conditions; the rate tells you how quickly you get there.
Industry must balance yield, rate and cost (see the Haber process).
Link to other topics: chemistry of the Haber process, 'Using resources', and economic and environmental decisions.
core.p: The **relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction**. This means that by changing temperature, pressure or concentration, chemists can change the **position of equilibrium**. If the equilibrium mixture contains a lot of product, we say the position lies to the right (favours the products); if it contains mostly reactant, the position lies to the left. The **yield** is the amount of product obtained compared with the maximum possible, so moving the position to the right increases the yield. The Higher tier rules for predicting the shift are covered in the next spec point (Le Chatelier's principle).

bullets: Method 1 (copper sulfate): heat a few crystals of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate in a test tube with a Bunsen burner until they turn white; water condenses at the top of the tube.
Let the tube cool, then add a few drops of water to the white solid: it turns blue and gets hot, showing the reverse reaction is exothermic.
Method 2 (ammonium chloride): heat a small amount of ammonium chloride at the bottom of a test tube; white solid disappears and re-forms as a white deposit higher up where it is cooler.
Hazards: hot glassware and burns, irritant gases (ammonia, hydrogen chloride), eye damage; control by eye protection, small amounts, clamping the tube at an angle and using a fume cupboard.
Observation words: 'blue to white', 'white to blue', 'white solid re-forms on cooler part of the tube'.
Conclusion wording: 'the reaction is reversible because the products can react to form the original reactants'.
These practicals show reversibility, but a true dynamic equilibrium needs a closed system, which is not the case in an open test tube.
core.p: Reversible reactions can be shown with simple practicals. In each case you see a change in one direction, then reverse the conditions and see the original substance return. The aim is to show that a reaction can go backwards, not to measure an equilibrium. Always include safety (eye protection; ammonium chloride heating gives off irritant gases, so do it in a fume cupboard or with a small amount).

bullets: Raw materials: nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas (methane) and steam.
Typical conditions: about 450 °C, 200 atmospheres pressure and an iron catalyst.
The reaction is reversible, so only part of the gases is converted to ammonia in one pass through the reactor.
Ammonia is removed by cooling it until it liquefies (its boiling point is higher than that of nitrogen and hydrogen).
Unreacted N2 and H2 are recycled so that nothing is wasted.
Removing ammonia pushes the position of equilibrium towards the products (see Le Chatelier).
The forward reaction is exothermic (-92 kJ/mol as written).
Link to other topics: Haber process in 'Using resources' (4.10) and fertilisers.
core.h: Dynamic equilibrium in industry: the Haber process
core.p: The Haber process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). Because the reaction is reversible, it never goes to completion in the reactor; the gas mixture leaving contains nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia in equilibrium. Ammonia is cooled and liquefied so it can be removed, and the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back into the reactor. This keeps the reaction making more ammonia, and it is an example of why understanding equilibrium matters economically. The details of the conditions are linked to Le Chatelier's principle in the Higher tier notes.

bullets: Equilibrium = equal rates, constant concentrations, closed system, dynamic.
A mixture at equilibrium will stay the same indefinitely if conditions stay the same.
If a closed system is not at equilibrium the concentrations are still changing.
At equilibrium both reactants and products are present (unless the reaction has gone to completion).
The same equilibrium mixture is reached from either direction at the same conditions.
If the equilibrium mixture is mostly product, the reaction is described as having a high yield under those conditions.
Higher tier link: Le Chatelier's principle lets you predict how the position shifts when you change concentration, temperature or pressure.
Use precise words: 'rate' not 'speed', 'concentration' not 'amount' when talking about constancy.
core.h: Common ideas that link everything together
core.p: Examiners often ask for explanation in terms of rates and concentrations, so bring together what you have learned. Equilibrium is a balance of rates, not a balance of amounts. Concentrations can be very uneven and still be constant. Equilibrium is only possible for a reversible reaction in a closed system. A catalyst does not change where equilibrium lies, only how quickly it is reached. Changing the conditions can change the position, because the rates of the forward and reverse reactions respond differently.

exam: Define dynamic equilibrium (2 marks): 'in a closed system, forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate' and 'concentrations of reactants and products stay constant'. Learn this as two marks.
Use the phrase 'closed system' whenever equilibrium is mentioned; it is often a separate mark point.
For 'state' or 'give' questions (1 mark) give a short phrase; for 'explain' questions (2 to 3 marks) link a cause to an effect with 'because', 'so' or 'therefore'.
Graph questions: read the time at which the lines become horizontal and quote it with units; say 'concentrations are constant' to describe the plateau.
Do not write that the reaction 'stops' at equilibrium; write 'there is no overall change' or 'concentrations stay constant' and mention both reactions continue.
Energy questions: always state that the reverse reaction transfers the same amount of energy but in the opposite sense (exothermic one way, endothermic the other).
For a 4 mark rate-time sketch: label axes, forward line starts high and falls, reverse starts at zero and rises, lines meet and then stay together and level.

6 mark questions use a level-of-response mark scheme: define equilibrium, mention closed system, explain rates equal, state concentrations constant, link to a given example (such as ammonia removal), and give a clear conclusion.
If asked to describe a practical showing reversibility, give observations in both directions (blue to white on heating, white to blue on adding water) and a safety point.
A catalyst question nearly always has the model answer: no effect on position; equilibrium reached faster; both rates increased equally.
Use the symbol ⇌ in any equation for a reversible reaction; using → loses the mark in many mark schemes.
Check the units in data questions (mol/dm3, s) and quote values read from the graph rather than writing vague statements.

mistakes.r: Both the forward and reverse reactions are still occurring, at the same rate (dynamic).
mistakes.w: At equilibrium the reaction has stopped.

mistakes.r: The concentrations are constant; they are not necessarily equal.
mistakes.w: At equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.

mistakes.r: At equilibrium reactants and products are both present.
mistakes.w: Equilibrium is reached when all the reactants are used up.

mistakes.r: Equilibrium needs a closed system so that reactants and products cannot escape.
mistakes.w: A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium in an open container.

mistakes.r: The rates are equal and greater than zero.
mistakes.w: The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are zero at equilibrium.

mistakes.r: A catalyst speeds up both reactions equally so equilibrium is reached sooner, but the position does not change.
mistakes.w: A catalyst increases the yield at equilibrium.

mistakes.r: The reverse reaction is endothermic and takes in exactly the same amount of energy.
mistakes.w: If the forward reaction is exothermic the reverse reaction gives out less energy.

mistakes.r: The amounts are constant because the forward and reverse rates are equal; the reactions are continuing.
mistakes.w: The amounts are not changing, so nothing is happening.

summary: In a closed system a reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant (but are not necessarily equal). You must know reversible reactions, their energy changes (exothermic one way, endothermic the other, same amount), and that the position of equilibrium depends on conditions; it matters because industrial processes such as the Haber process rely on it.

terms.d: A reaction in which the products can react to form the original reactants.
The reaction in which reactants are converted to products (left to right in the equation).
The reaction in which products are converted back to reactants (right to left).
The symbol used in an equation to show that a reaction is reversible.
A system in which no reactants or products can escape and nothing can enter.
A system in which matter, such as a gas, can escape from the reaction vessel.
In a closed system, the state in which the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
The relative amounts of reactants and products in the equilibrium mixture, which depend on the conditions.
The amount of product obtained compared with the maximum amount that could be obtained.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
A crystalline compound containing water of crystallisation, such as blue copper(II) sulfate crystals.
A substance that contains no water of crystallisation, such as white copper(II) sulfate powder.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up; in equilibrium it speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally.
The amount of a substance in a given volume of solution or gas, for example in mol/dm3 or g/dm3.

worked.ans: Equilibrium is reached by 40 s because the concentrations are constant afterwards (A = 0.40, B = 0.60 mol/dm3). The position lies to the right because there is more B (product) than A.
worked.q: The concentrations of A and B in the reaction A ⇌ B in a closed container were measured. At 0 s [A] = 1.00 and [B] = 0.00 mol/dm3. At 20 s [A] = 0.55, [B] = 0.45. At 40 s [A] = 0.40, [B] = 0.60. At 60 s [A] = 0.40, [B] = 0.60. At 80 s [A] = 0.40, [B] = 0.60. State whether and when equilibrium has been reached, and where the position lies. (3 marks)
steps: Look for the time when the concentrations stop changing: they are the same at 40, 60 and 80 s.
So equilibrium was reached by 40 s (between 20 s and 40 s it had not yet been reached, as the values were still changing).
Compare the amounts: [B] = 0.60 is greater than [A] = 0.40, so more product than reactant is present.
Check the total: 0.40 + 0.60 = 1.00, which is the starting amount of A, so the numbers are consistent.

worked.ans: Ammonium chloride decomposes on heating into ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases, NH4Cl ⇌ NH3 + HCl. These gases recombine on the cooler part of the tube to re-form solid ammonium chloride, so the products have reacted to make the original reactant, which shows the reaction is reversible.
worked.q: A student heats ammonium chloride in a test tube and sees white solid appear higher up the tube. Explain what this shows and why it can be called a reversible reaction. (3 marks)
steps: On heating, NH4Cl breaks down into NH3 and HCl gases (forward reaction).
The gases move up the tube where it is cooler.
There they react together and form white ammonium chloride solid again (reverse reaction).
So the products have formed the original reactant: this is the definition of a reversible reaction.

worked.ans: The forward and reverse reactions are both still occurring but at exactly the same rate, so reactants are made as fast as they are used up and the concentrations stay constant.
worked.q: Explain why, at dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations in a closed system remain constant even though the reactions have not stopped. (2 marks)
steps: Identify that both the forward and reverse reactions are still happening.
State that the rates are equal.
Link: the reactant used by the forward reaction is replaced at the same rate by the reverse reaction, so no overall change.
